Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. By Anabel Sosa (https://www.sfgate.com/author/anabel-sosa/) , Senior California politics reporter Oct 30, 2026
An election worker prepares “I Voted” stickers at a vote center in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles on Oct. 25, 2026.

California’s proposed billionaire tax (https://www.instagram.com/p/De-k5diTsMR/) has commanded most of this election’s attention, but a less-talked-about tax measure appears to be one of the few statewide tax propositions that is likely to succeed.
A recent poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408) from UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies released Thursday found Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm) is likely to pass, with 54% of likely voters saying they plan to vote yes, while 37% said they plan to vote no. It is the only measure out of seven that were surveyed that had more than 50% approval.

Prop. 3 is a tax measure that would make higher income tax rates permanent for single people who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $742,000. It would make permanent the existing tax rates, which are set to expire after 2030. If passed, 89% of tax revenue will continue to fund K-12 schools and the remaining 11% will go to community colleges.
These increased tax rates were initially passed by voters in 2012 during a budget deficit, and were extended by voters in 2016.
Each year, the high-income tax rates bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion for the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). The revenue has ranged year to year depending on earnings from the stock market and other outside factors. For those who earn over $1 million, that tax has been on top of another existing 1% tax that goes toward mental health services.

MediaNews Group/Getty Images David Goldberg, the president of the California Teachers Association, which supports the proposition, told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) that if the measure doesn’t pass, about 50,000 teachers could be laid off.

The ballot measure also has support from the National Education Association and the California School Employees Association. The opposition includes the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
While Prop. 3 appears to be gliding toward a win, polls are showing that Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, is on track for failure. That measure would impose a new, one-time 5% tax on the financial assets of anyone who is worth $1 billion or more. If passed, 90% of the money would go toward funding healthcare to make up for an estimated $30 billion California (https://www.chcf.org/blog/2025/10/03/how-massive-federal-cuts-will-create-unprecedented-challenges-medi-cal-patients-providers/) will lose every year for Medicaid after Congress cut funding. Another 10 % would go to public education, food assistance and administration of the tax.
Prop. 40 has seen support drop in recent weeks (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/polling-proposition-40-22496894.php) as billionaire-funded opposition efforts ramped up. The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday that found the measure only has 46% of voters in favor of the billionaire tax. Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that only 44% of voters are in support.
A hand holds a political mailer about California Proposition 40, a November 2026 ballot measure proposing a one-time tax on billionaires, in Reliez Valley, California, Oct. 23, 2026.
Gado/Getty Images The No on Prop. 40 campaign has been primarily bankrolled by a political action committee called Building a Better California that was formed this year, largely focused on blocking the measure, according (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767) to state finance disclosures. With contributors like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and billionaire investor John Doerr, the group has raised over $333 million, mostly going toward opposing Prop. 40 and supporting propositions 41 and 42, which would nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php), making it one of the highest-funded ballot initiative efforts (https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/10/26/with-798-9-million-in-contributions-and-counting-2026-is-the-most-expensive-ballot-measure-election-cycle-in-california/) in California history.

Gavin Newsom and other Democrats, would block new taxes on the ownership of most financial assets, and would block new state taxes that apply retroactively to taxpayer conduct.

PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Makes permanent the existing 2012 voter-approved tax rates for high-income Californians, currently set to expire in 2031.
Rates apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers, $742,000 for joint filers, and $505,000 for heads of household (2025 levels; adjusted annually for inflation).
Allocates tax revenues 89% to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges.
Allows local school boards to decide how revenues are spent; bars use for administrative costs.
Increases General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves, and other programs.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS, HEALTHCARE AND OUR COMMUNITIES WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES.
Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone. Prop. 3 prevents millionaires and billionaires from getting a tax cut, and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms.
PROP. 3 PREVENTS BILLIONS IN CUTS TO OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE.
Without Prop. 3, California’s 8 million public school and community college students face billions in cuts, including teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and bigger class sizes. Families could lose access to preventive healthcare and affordable prescription drugs, and the Medi-Cal coverage that millions of Californians rely on could be put at risk.
PROP. 3 ONLY EXTENDS THE CURRENT TAX RATES ON THE WEALTHIEST TOP 2%.
Prop. 3 maintains the income tax rates that the wealthiest Californians have paid for the past 15 years. If those tax rates are allowed to expire, it would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities. Proposition 3 keeps the existing rates on the top 2% of incomes.
GUARANTEES THE MONEY REACHES THE CLASSROOM— NOT SACRAMENTO.
Proposition 3 includes Constitutional protections and tough accountability. It guarantees that funds from Proposition 3 go directly to local schools—the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it, redirect it, or spend a single dollar on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Prop. 3’s school guarantee then frees up billions that help fund Medi-Cal for children, seniors and families.
Every dollar in Prop. 3 is independently audited every year and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties. Local school districts must post annual accounting online to guarantee that Californians know exactly how and where funds are spent.
PROP. 3 SECURES OUR CHILDREN’S FUTURE.
For more than a decade, these revenues have helped fund critical programs California families and communities count on—from school lunches, smaller class sizes and mental health counselors to children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal. They’ve also helped stave off cuts during economic downturns by investing more in the state’s Rainy Day Fund, protecting our schools and healthcare when the economy slows. Proposition 3 keeps that progress going for the next generation.
PROP. 3 IS SUPPORTED BY TEACHERS, NURSES, AND HEALTHCARE WORKERS.
Yes on 3 is supported by:
California State PTA
California Federation of Teachers
California Nurses Association
California School Employees Association
California School Nurses Organization
California Teachers Association
Community College League of California
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
The educators in our classrooms and the nurses who care for our kids all agree: Vote YES on Proposition 3. Let’s protect what matters most, without raising your taxes. Vote YES on Proposition 3.
www.YesProp3CA.com
David Goldberg , President
California Teachers Association
Katie Nilsson , RN, President
California School Nurses Organization
Jodi Hicks , President
Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3
NO ON PROP. 3—STOP PERMANENTLY HIGHER INCOME TAXES
In 2012, politicians and special interests promised Californians that their income tax increases would be TEMPORARY. Now they’re claiming that making those taxes permanent somehow ISN’T a tax increase at all. Don’t buy it. Prop. 3 locks in what would become the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history— costing taxpayers up to $15 billion every year.
NO ON PROP. 3—REMIND POLITICIANS WHAT “TEMPORARY” MEANS
Temporary: lasting for a limited time only; not permanent.
California taxpayers kept their end of the bargain—paying temporary higher income taxes for 16 years. Politicians should keep theirs and stop pushing for even higher taxes.
NO ON PROP. 3—STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING
Prop. 3 does nothing to stop the waste, fraud and reckless spending that turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion deficit in just three years. If Sacramento had spent responsibly, they wouldn’t be asking taxpayers to make “temporary” taxes permanent.
NO ON PROP. 3—DON’T MAKE CALIFORNIA EVEN MORE EXPENSIVE
Californians have the highest cost of living and pay the highest income, sales and gas taxes in America. Making a temporary tax permanent only makes California more expensive.
NO ON PROP. 3—FIX THE SPENDING PROBLEM FIRST
California doesn’t have a tax revenue problem—it has a spending problem. California’s population grew by less than 2% in the past decade while the politicians doubled spending. Say no to permanently higher taxes. Join us to oppose higher income taxes at VoteNoProp3.com .
NO ON PROP. 3

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 3
PROP. 3-TURNS "TEMPORARY" TAXES INTO PERMANENT HIGHER INCOME TAXES
Sacramento politicians make big promises to get our support for higher taxes. Then they spend our tax dollars with no accountability-losing billions to waste, fraud and overspending.
Take Prop. 3. Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary-only for seven years to cover a budget deficit. Then those "temporary" taxes were extended for another 12 years with the promise to voters that the higher taxes would solve the problems the politicians created. Now the special interests and politicians want to make these higher income taxes PERMANENT.
California voters should say NO to PERMANENTLY higher income taxes.
PROP. 3-HIGHER INCOME TAXES = HIGHER COST OF LIVING
Californians have the nation's highest cost of living partly because we also suffer from the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes of all fifty states. The same politicians also gave us the highest gasoline prices in the nation, higher insurance costs, higher utility costs, higher food costs, and higher housing costs. Now they want to make higher income taxes permanent, while adding new taxes on your health insurance, new taxes on software-and they are even considering a "jobs" tax. Say NO to INCREASING our cost of living with higher taxes.
PROP. 3-VOTERS DESERVE REAL RESULTS, NOT BROKEN PROMISES
Waste, fraud and overspending by state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.
The politicians and special interests promised temporary income taxes were needed to avoid big cuts to government programs. Since the "temporary" increases were first passed, government spending has increased by $150 billion-a more than 2.5X increase. Over the same time period, our schools, infrastructure and public safety have gotten worse. Say NO to endless broken promises.
NO ON PROP. 3-STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING
The politicians and special interests turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years. They mismanaged our tax dollars so badly, they now want voters to bail them out with permanently higher taxes.
Say NO to $100 billion wasted on a train to nowhere.
Say NO to $37 billion wasted on homeless programs that don't work.
Say NO to $31 billion wasted on unemployment fraud.
NO ON PROP. 3-FIX SACRAMENTO'S SPENDING PROBLEM BEFORE RAISING TAXES
California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem. California's population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.
It's not just state taxes that keep going up. Politicians and special interests have imposed more than 2,000 new local tax increases in just the past ten years-making it much harder for struggling Californians to make ends meet.
Californians shouldn't support any higher taxes until we get spending under control.
STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING.
NO NEW TAXES.
NO ON PROP. 3.

PROPOSITION 3
Proposition 3 protects our schools, our healthcare and our communities—without raising your taxes.
PROP. 3 KEEPS THE TAX RATES THE TOP 2% HAVE PAID FOR THE PAST 15 YEARS AND DOES NOT RAISE YOUR TAXES.
Prop. 3 maintains the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% of Californians have been paying for 15 years, ensuring couples that earn more than $740,000 continue to pay their fair share.
WITHOUT PROP. 3 MILLIONAIRES AND BILLIONAIRES GET A MASSIVE TAX CUT—AND THE REST OF US PAY FOR IT.
Teacher and staff layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and fewer counselors in our schools; cuts to Medi-Cal, children’s healthcare and the clinics families rely on; and less for the firefighters, emergency response and wildfire protection that keep our communities safe.

Prop. 3’s funding goes straight to local schools and community colleges. Sacramento politicians cannot touch it or redirect it. Not one penny may be spent on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. PROP. 3 PROTECTS HEALTHCARE AND FIRE PROTECTION.

## What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030.

The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.

What does California Proposition 3 do?
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
The tax has been a vital source of revenue for schools. Supporters say if Prop. 3 fails, the loss of up to $15 billion a year for schools will likely lead to layoffs, program cuts and other reductions.

Arguments against
Opponents point out that California already has some of the highest income taxes in the country. They say the measure may spur wealthy Californians to leave for lower-tax states, taking jobs and revenue with them.

PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. While Prop. 40 flounders, another progressive tax in California is looking likely
By Anabel Sosa (https://www.sfgate.com/author/anabel-sosa/) , Senior California politics reporter Oct 30, 2026
An election worker prepares “I Voted” stickers at a vote center in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles on Oct. 25, 2026.
Michael Yanow/NurPhoto/Getty Images
California’s proposed billionaire tax (https://www.instagram.com/p/De-k5diTsMR/) has commanded most of this election’s attention, but a less-talked-about tax measure appears to be one of the few statewide tax propositions that is likely to succeed.
A recent poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408) from UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies released Thursday found Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm) is likely to pass, with 54% of likely voters saying they plan to vote yes, while 37% said they plan to vote no. It is the only measure out of seven that were surveyed that had more than 50% approval.

Article continues below this ad
Prop. 3 is a tax measure that would make higher income tax rates permanent for single people who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $742,000. It would make permanent the existing tax rates, which are set to expire after 2030. If passed, 89% of tax revenue will continue to fund K-12 schools and the remaining 11% will go to community colleges.
These increased tax rates were initially passed by voters in 2012 during a budget deficit, and were extended by voters in 2016.
Each year, the high-income tax rates bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion for the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). The revenue has ranged year to year depending on earnings from the stock market and other outside factors. For those who earn over $1 million, that tax has been on top of another existing 1% tax that goes toward mental health services.
Former LAUSD Superintendent Austin Beutner, who founded Vision To Learn 12 years ago, is flanked by Sherlett Hendy Newbill, LAUSD School Board member, and David Goldberg, president of California Teachers Association, as Vision To Learn gives out its 300,000th pair of glasses in California at 24th Street Elementary School in Los Angeles on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026.
MediaNews Group/Getty Images David Goldberg, the president of the California Teachers Association, which supports the proposition, told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) that if the measure doesn’t pass, about 50,000 teachers could be laid off.
Advertisement

The ballot measure also has support from the National Education Association and the California School Employees Association. The opposition includes the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
While Prop. 3 appears to be gliding toward a win, polls are showing that Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, is on track for failure. That measure would impose a new, one-time 5% tax on the financial assets of anyone who is worth $1 billion or more. If passed, 90% of the money would go toward funding healthcare to make up for an estimated $30 billion California (https://www.chcf.org/blog/2025/10/03/how-massive-federal-cuts-will-create-unprecedented-challenges-medi-cal-patients-providers/) will lose every year for Medicaid after Congress cut funding. Another 10 % would go to public education, food assistance and administration of the tax.
Prop. 40 has seen support drop in recent weeks (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/polling-proposition-40-22496894.php) as billionaire-funded opposition efforts ramped up. The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday that found the measure only has 46% of voters in favor of the billionaire tax. Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that only 44% of voters are in support.
A hand holds a political mailer about California Proposition 40, a November 2026 ballot measure proposing a one-time tax on billionaires, in Reliez Valley, California, Oct. 23, 2026.
Gado/Getty Images The No on Prop. 40 campaign has been primarily bankrolled by a political action committee called Building a Better California that was formed this year, largely focused on blocking the measure, according (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767) to state finance disclosures. With contributors like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and billionaire investor John Doerr, the group has raised over $333 million, mostly going toward opposing Prop. 40 and supporting propositions 41 and 42, which would nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php), making it one of the highest-funded ballot initiative efforts (https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/10/26/with-798-9-million-in-contributions-and-counting-2026-is-the-most-expensive-ballot-measure-election-cycle-in-california/) in California history.

Proposition 41 would require audits of special statewide taxes and prohibit certain types of new taxes, and Proposition 42, which is endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and other Democrats, would block new taxes on the ownership of most financial assets, and would block new state taxes that apply retroactively to taxpayer conduct.
The Institute of Governmental Studies poll released Thursday surveyed 2,787 registered voters, of which 1,477 had either already voted in the midterm election or were considered likely to vote. It was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19 through Oct. 25, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.
